questions.prompt: Which sentence follows the rubric requiring a comma after an introductory dependent clause, an ellipsis to indicate a trailing thought at the end of a sentence, and an em dash to add emphasis before a final independent clause?
choices: After the storm passed, she stared at the horizon... the sun finally broke through.
After the storm passed she stared at the horizon...—the sun finally broke through.
After the storm passed, she stared at the horizon.—the sun finally broke through.
After the storm passed, she stared at the horizon...—the sun finally broke through.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence uses a comma after the introductory dependent clause, ends the main clause with an ellipsis to show a trailing thought, and follows it with an em dash that emphasizes the final independent clause.
questions.skill: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that follows a rubric demanding a pair of commas to set off a nonrestrictive clause, an ellipsis omitting words in the middle of a quotation, and a dash to add emphasis before the final clause.
choices: The author who won the prize, said, "The story... matters"—and the audience listened.
The author, who won the prize, said, "The story... matters"—and the audience listened.
The author, who won the prize said, "The story... matters"—and the audience listened.
The author, who won the prize, said, "The story... matters" and the audience listened.
questions.explanation: The first option correctly uses commas around the nonrestrictive clause, an ellipsis inside the quotation to show omitted words, and an em dash before the final clause for emphasis.
questions.skill: punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that follows a rubric requiring an ellipsis to show an omission at the end of a clause, a dash to add emphasis before the final clause, and commas separating items in a series where the last item is omitted and marked by the ellipsis.
choices: She gathered apples, oranges, bananas...—the fruit was fresh, and served them.
She gathered apples, oranges, bananas... the fruit was fresh—and served them.
She gathered apples, oranges, bananas...—the fruit was fresh—and served them.
She gathered apples, oranges, bananas—the fruit was fresh...—and served them.
questions.explanation: Only the first sentence includes the series commas, the terminal ellipsis, and the emphatic dash before the concluding clause.
questions.skill: Rubric-based punctuation evaluation
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to stand for an omitted alternative within a quoted question?
choices: Do you have the map, the printed version?
Do you have the map; the printed version?
Do you have the map—the printed version?
Do you have the map... the printed version?
questions.explanation: The ellipsis represents the omitted alternative expressed by or before the second option, the printed version.
questions.skill: Using ellipses for omitted alternatives
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show that the end of a list has been deliberately omitted?
choices: After packing her sketchbook, Maya realized she had also forgotten her eraser, colored pencils, and...
After packing her sketchbook, Maya realized she had also forgotten her eraser, colored pencils, and—
After packing her sketchbook, Maya realized she had also forgotten her eraser, colored pencils, and,
After packing her sketchbook, Maya realized she had also forgotten her eraser, colored pencils, and:
questions.explanation: The ellipsis after and indicates that the list of forgotten items is deliberately left unfinished.
questions.skill: Recognizing ellipses for omitted endings
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a dash to mark an abrupt break within a quotation and a comma to separate two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction?
choices: "We need to move—now," Priya said, and the team grabbed its equipment.
"We need to move now," Priya said—and the team grabbed its equipment.
"We need to move—now," Priya said and the team grabbed its equipment.
"We need to move... now," Priya said, and the team grabbed its equipment.
questions.explanation: The em dash creates an abrupt break within the quotation, and the comma before and correctly separates two independent clauses.
questions.skill: Combining an internal dash with coordinating-clause punctuation
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to indicate an omission at the end of a clause, an em dash to insert an abrupt interruption, and a comma before a coordinating conjunction?
choices: She promised to finish the report... the deadline passed—and the client called.
She promised to finish the report... the deadline passed, and the client called.
She promised to finish the report—... the deadline passed, and the client called.
She promised to finish the report...—the deadline passed, and the client called.
questions.explanation: The first option contains an ellipsis at the end of the clause, an em dash that abruptly interrupts the flow, and a comma before the coordinating conjunction "and."
questions.skill: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that follows the rubric by using an ellipsis for omitted material in the middle of a sentence, a pair of dashes to set off an appositive, and a comma before a coordinating conjunction.
choices: The manuscript—an early draft... was revised, and the editor approved it.
The manuscript—an early draft...—was revised, and the editor approved it.
The manuscript—an early draft...—was revised and the editor approved it.
The manuscript—an early draft...—was revised; and the editor approved it.
questions.explanation: Option A encloses the appositive with a pair of em dashes, places an ellipsis inside the appositive to show omitted material, and uses a comma before the coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses.
questions.skill: Punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly punctuates a question within a quotation and uses a dash to introduce an interrupting action?
choices: 'Did you finish the map,' the guide asked—then he pointed north.
'Did you finish the map?' the guide asked—then he pointed north.
'Did you finish the map' the guide asked—then he pointed north.
'Did you finish the map?' the guide asked, then he pointed north.
questions.explanation: A question mark completes the quoted question, no comma is needed before the attribution, and the em dash introduces the interrupting action.
questions.skill: Punctuating quotations and introducing interruptions with dashes
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence follows the rubric requiring a pair of commas to set off a nonrestrictive clause, an ellipsis to omit the final item in a series, and a dash to introduce an abrupt interruption?
choices: My sister, who loves hiking, packed water, snacks, maps...—then the trail vanished.
My sister who loves hiking packed water, snacks, maps...—then the trail vanished.
My sister, who loves hiking, packed water, snacks, maps—then the trail vanished.
My sister, who loves hiking, packed water, snacks, maps... then the trail vanished.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence sets off the nonrestrictive clause with commas, uses an ellipsis to omit the last item in the series, and employs a dash to introduce the abrupt interruption.
questions.skill: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two contrasting independent clauses?
choices: The runners reached the hill but, the storm forced them to stop.
The runners reached the hill; but the storm forced them to stop.
The runners reached the hill, but the storm forced them to stop.
The runners reached the hill: but the storm forced them to stop.
questions.explanation: The comma before but correctly separates the two independent clauses while showing their contrast.
questions.skill: Applying commas between independent clauses
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence meets a rubric requiring a comma after an introductory dependent clause, a dash for an abrupt interruption, and an ellipsis showing omitted words in a quotation?
choices: When the lights flickered the projector stopped—the audience groaned—and the teacher said, “Wait... give me a minute.”
When the lights flickered, the projector stopped, the audience groaned, and the teacher said, “Wait... give me a minute.”
When the lights flickered, the projector stopped—the audience groaned—and the teacher said, “Wait, give me a minute.”
When the lights flickered, the projector stopped—the audience groaned—and the teacher said, “Wait... give me a minute.”
questions.explanation: This sentence correctly includes a comma after the introductory clause, uses paired em dashes around the interruption, and shows omitted words with an ellipsis in the quotation.
questions.skill: Selecting punctuation that fulfills multiple criteria
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence that meets a rubric calling for matching commas around a nonrestrictive clause, an ellipsis omitting words in the middle of a quotation, and an em dash setting off an explanatory interruption after the quotation.
choices: The author, who won the prize, said, 'The story... ends quietly', a reminder that silence speaks.
The author who won the prize, said, 'The story... ends quietly'—a reminder that silence speaks.
The author, who won the prize, said, 'The story ends quietly'—a reminder that silence speaks.
The author, who won the prize, said, 'The story... ends quietly'—a reminder that silence speaks.
questions.explanation: The first sentence correctly encloses the nonrestrictive clause in commas, uses an ellipsis inside the quote, and follows the quote with an em dash introducing the explanation.
questions.skill: Rubric-based punctuation evaluation
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Evaluate Example 3: My neighbor, a retired pilot, called, 'The sky is clearing—wait, the storm is coming!' Which rubric feedback is accurate?
choices: The sentence uses matching commas for the nonrestrictive appositive and a dash to mark the interruption in the quoted speech.
The sentence uses matching dashes for the nonrestrictive appositive and a comma to mark the interruption in the quoted speech.
The sentence uses matching commas for the restrictive appositive and an ellipsis to mark the interruption in the quoted speech.
The sentence needs no commas around the nonrestrictive appositive and uses a dash to mark an omission in the quoted speech.
questions.explanation: The feedback correctly recognizes both the matching commas around the nonrestrictive appositive and the dash indicating an interruption in the quoted speech.
questions.skill: Evaluating punctuation against a writing rubric
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses matching commas to set off a nonrestrictive clause that adds information?
choices: The river, which flooded the lower road forced the hikers to turn back.
The river which flooded the lower road, forced the hikers to turn back.
The river, which flooded the lower road, forced the hikers to turn back.
The river which flooded the lower road forced the hikers to turn back.
questions.explanation: The clause which flooded the lower road is nonrestrictive, so matching commas correctly set it off as additional information.
questions.skill: Distinguishing restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: A student writes: After the storm passed, the guide—a retired ranger—said, “We should continue...” Which rubric feedback is accurate?
choices: The sentence misses the rubric because the ellipsis shows that the speaker completed the thought rather than leaving it unfinished.
The sentence misses the rubric because the appositive is correctly enclosed by paired commas, making the em dashes unnecessary.
The sentence meets the rubric because the introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma, the appositive is enclosed by paired em dashes, and the ellipsis marks an unfinished thought.
The sentence misses the rubric because the introductory dependent clause is correctly followed by a dash rather than a comma.
questions.explanation: The sentence satisfies all three rubric requirements by using the required comma, paired em dashes, and ellipsis in their intended functions.
questions.skill: Checking a written sentence against punctuation criteria
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: The draft reads: The guide said, 'Take the north trail... it is clearer,' and when rain began the hikers followed the map. Which revision best fixes it so it meets the rubric for an ellipsis showing omitted words, paired dashes setting off an interruption, and a comma joining two independent clauses?
choices: The guide said, 'Take the north trail... it is clearer' and when rain began the hikers followed the map.
The guide said, 'Take the north trail... it is clearer,' and—when the rain began—the hikers followed the map.
The guide said, 'Take the north trail... it is clearer,' and when rain began, the hikers followed the map.
The guide said, 'Take the north trail... it is clearer,' and when rain began the hikers—followed the map.
questions.explanation: This revision uses the ellipsis to leave a connection unstated, pairs dashes around the interruption, and places a comma before and to join the two independent clauses.
questions.skill: Rubric check combining ellipses, dashes, and commas
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly follows a rubric requiring a comma after an introductory dependent clause, paired dashes around an appositive, and an ellipsis showing hesitation?
choices: Before the audition Lena said, 'I am ready... probably.' The judge—the sponsor's assistant—watched from the balcony.
Before the audition, Lena said, 'I am ready... probably.' The judge, the sponsor's assistant, watched from the balcony.
Before the audition, Lena said, 'I am ready... probably.' The judge—the sponsor's assistant—watched from the balcony.
Before the audition, Lena said, 'I am ready... probably.' The judge—the sponsor's assistant watched from the balcony.
questions.explanation: The comma after the introductory dependent clause, the paired dashes around the appositive, and the ellipsis inside the quotation each meet the stated rubric.
questions.skill: Rubric check for dependent-clause commas, paired dashes, and hesitation ellipses
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses commas to separate items in a series where the final item is omitted and indicated by an ellipsis, and a pair of dashes to insert a parenthetical comment?
choices: She packed socks, shirts, pants... (the essentials) and left.
She packed socks, shirts, pants...—the essentials, and left.
She packed socks, shirts, pants...—the essentials—and left.
She packed socks, shirts, pants... the essentials—and left.
questions.explanation: Option A shows a series separated by commas with an ellipsis indicating the omitted final item, and it correctly surrounds the parenthetical comment with a pair of em dashes.
questions.skill: Punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis immediately after an opening quotation mark to represent omitted introductory words?
choices: Lena said, "We can meet at seven if the library is open..."
Lena said... "We can meet at seven if the library is open."
Lena said, "We can meet at seven if the library is open."
Lena said, "...we can meet at seven if the library is open."
questions.explanation: The ellipsis appears directly after the opening quotation mark and signals that introductory words have been omitted before we can meet at seven.
questions.skill: Showing omitted words with an ellipsis
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows an ellipsis marking a pause within a quoted thought, a pair of dashes signaling an abrupt shift, and a comma setting off a nonrestrictive clause?
choices: 'I wonder...' she paused—if the train will arrive, which is uncertain, on time.
'I wonder...'—she paused—if the train will arrive, which is uncertain, on time.
'I wonder...'—she paused if the train will arrive, which is uncertain, on time.
'I wonder...'—she paused—if the train will arrive which is uncertain on time.
questions.explanation: The first option contains an ellipsis inside the quotation, a pair of dashes surrounding "she paused" to mark an abrupt shift, and commas that set off the nonrestrictive clause "which is uncertain."
questions.skill: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly encloses a nonrestrictive appositive in a matching pair of commas?
choices: Her brother a medical student, volunteered to demonstrate the procedure.
Her brother; a medical student, volunteered to demonstrate the procedure.
Her brother, a medical student, volunteered to demonstrate the procedure.
Her brother, a medical student volunteered to demonstrate the procedure.
questions.explanation: The appositive a medical student is nonrestrictive, so it is correctly enclosed by a matching pair of commas.
questions.skill: Commas with a nonrestrictive appositive
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory dependent clause, paired dashes to set off an appositive, and an ellipsis to show omitted words in the middle of a quotation?
choices: After the briefing ended, the coordinator—the visiting archivist—said, 'We begin... the second phase.'
After the briefing ended the coordinator—the visiting archivist—said, 'We begin... the second phase.'
After the briefing ended, the coordinator—the visiting archivist said, 'We begin... the second phase.'
After the briefing ended, the coordinator—the visiting archivist—said, 'We begin the second phase...'
questions.explanation: The sentence has the required comma after the introductory dependent clause, matching dashes around the appositive, and an ellipsis showing omitted words inside the quotation.
questions.skill: Applying punctuation to a writing rubric
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory interjection and a dash to emphasize an urgent instruction?
choices: Oh; the train is approaching—turn around!
Oh the train is approaching—turn around!
Oh, the train is approaching—turn around!
Oh, the train is approaching - turn around!
questions.explanation: The comma correctly follows the introductory interjection Oh, and the em dash emphasizes the urgent instruction turn around.
questions.skill: Punctuation after interjections and dashes for emphasis
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence satisfies a rubric that requires a comma after an introductory dependent clause, a pair of dashes around an appositive, and an ellipsis at the end of a quotation to show a trailing thought?
choices: After the meeting ended, the manager—a seasoned pilot—said, 'We will review the data...'
After the meeting ended, the manager, a seasoned pilot, said, 'We will review the data...'
After the meeting ended the manager—a seasoned pilot—said, 'We will review the data...'
After the meeting ended, the manager—a seasoned pilot—said, 'We will review the data.'
questions.explanation: The first option includes the required introductory comma, the appositive set off by matching dashes, and an ellipsis at the end of the quoted material.
questions.skill: Rubric-based punctuation evaluation
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence best follows the rubric by using an ellipsis for an omission, a dash for an interruption, and a comma to mark a pause?
choices: Maya said, Come to the station at eight... She checked the map—the north entrance was closed—and chose another route, then headed toward the south gate.
Maya said, Come to the station at eight... She checked the map, the north entrance was closed, and chose another route, then headed toward the south gate.
Maya said, Come to the station at eight: She checked the map—the north entrance was closed—and chose another route, then headed toward the south gate.
Maya said, Come to the station at eight— She checked the map—the north entrance was closed—and chose another route, then headed toward the south gate.
questions.explanation: This version uses an ellipsis for the unfinished instruction, a dash to interrupt with route information, and a comma before then to mark a brief pause.
questions.skill: Combining ellipses, dashes, and commas in original writing
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which revision best follows a rubric requiring a comma after an introductory dependent clause and a dash to set off an explanatory interruption?
choices: Although the lights flickered the projection continued—barely visible on the screen.
Although the lights flickered, the projection continued, barely visible on the screen.
Although the lights flickered, the projection continued—barely visible on the screen.
Although the lights flickered the projection continued, barely visible on the screen.
questions.explanation: This revision correctly separates the introductory dependent clause with a comma and uses a dash to set off the explanatory phrase.
questions.skill: Revising introductory clauses and explanatory dashes
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that uses a comma after an introductory prepositional phrase, an ellipsis to show a trailing thought, and an em dash to insert an abrupt interruption before the final clause.
choices: In the quiet hallway she whispered...—the lights flickered, and the door slammed.
At dawn the hikers paused...—the storm broke, yet they continued.
In the quiet hallway, she whispered...—the lights flickered, and the door slammed.
In the quiet hallway, she whispered... the lights flickered, and the door slammed.
questions.explanation: The first sentence begins with the introductory prepositional phrase "In the quiet hallway," follows it with a comma, uses an ellipsis after "whispered" to indicate a trailing thought, and employs a single em dash before the final clause "the lights flickered, and the door slammed."
questions.skill: Identify correct punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which candidate fully satisfies a rubric requiring a comma after an introductory dependent clause, paired dashes around an appositive, and an ellipsis for omitted material in the middle of a quotation?
choices: Before the interview began, the candidate—a nervous junior—said, “I studied chemistry, biology, and physics...”
Before the interview began the candidate—a nervous junior—said, “I studied chemistry, biology... and physics.”
Before the interview began, the candidate, a nervous junior, said, “I studied chemistry, biology... and physics.”
Before the interview began, the candidate—a nervous junior—said, “I studied chemistry, biology... and physics.”
questions.explanation: The correct candidate places a comma after the introductory dependent clause, uses paired dashes around the appositive, and puts an ellipsis between omitted and stated items in the quotation.
questions.skill: Checking a sentence against a punctuation rubric
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which candidate best follows a rubric requiring a comma after an introductory participial phrase, an em dash to set off an explanatory interruption, and an ellipsis for a trailing thought in dialogue?
choices: Staring at the error message Maya whispered, "We should restart..."—the laptop had frozen.
Staring at the error message, Maya whispered, "We should restart..."—the laptop had frozen.
Staring at the error message, Maya whispered—"We should restart..." the laptop had frozen.
Staring at the error message, Maya whispered, "We should restart"—the laptop had frozen...
questions.explanation: The introductory participial phrase is followed by a comma, the ellipsis marks the trailing quoted thought, and the em dash sets off the explanatory interruption.
questions.skill: Checking introductory, dialogue, and explanatory punctuation
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that uses a comma after an introductory dependent clause, an ellipsis to omit words in the middle of a quotation, and a pair of dashes to enclose an interrupting phrase.
choices: After the meeting ended she said, 'We must decide... now'—the deadline loomed—and the team agreed.
After the meeting ended, she said, 'We must decide... now'—the deadline loomed—and the team agreed.
After the meeting ended, she said, 'We must decide now'—the deadline loomed—and the team agreed.
After the meeting ended, she said, 'We must decide... now'—the deadline loomed, and the team agreed.
questions.explanation: The first sentence begins with the dependent clause "After the meeting ended," follows it with a comma, includes an ellipsis inside the quotation to show omitted words, and surrounds the interrupting phrase "the deadline loomed" with a pair of dashes.
questions.skill: Identify correct punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma after an introductory clause, an ellipsis to show hesitation, and an em dash to add emphasis before the final clause?
choices: After the meeting ended, she hesitated...—the decision was final.
After the meeting ended she hesitated...—the decision was final.
After the meeting ended, she hesitated—the decision was final...
After the meeting ended, she hesitated... the decision was final.
questions.explanation: The first option places a comma after the introductory clause, uses an ellipsis to indicate hesitation, and follows it with an em dash that emphasizes the concluding clause.
questions.skill: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses and a dash to emphasize the final phrase?
choices: The rehearsal ran late but the choir still finished—exactly on time.
The rehearsal, ran late, but the choir still finished—exactly on time.
The rehearsal ran late, but the choir still finished - exactly on time.
The rehearsal ran late, but the choir still finished—exactly on time.
questions.explanation: The comma joins two independent clauses with but, and the em dash emphasizes the phrase exactly on time.
questions.skill: Comma splices, coordinating conjunctions, and dashes for emphasis
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an em dash to mark an interruption inside a quotation?
choices: "We need to le—" Lina grabbed her coat and ran.
"We need to leave:" Lina grabbed her coat and ran.
"We need to leave," Lina grabbed her coat and ran.
"We need to leave." Lina grabbed her coat—and ran.
questions.explanation: The em dash inside the quotation captures the speaker's abrupt interruption after le and also functions as the closing punctuation.
questions.skill: Em dash for an interrupted quotation
questions.topic: Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Identify the sentence that uses commas to separate items in a series, an ellipsis to omit the final item, and a pair of dashes to set off an appositive describing the series.
choices: She packed socks, shirts, pants...—her essential clothing—and left for the trip.
She packed socks, shirts, pants...—her essential clothing, and left for the trip.
She packed socks, shirts, pants—her essential clothing... and left for the trip.
She packed socks, shirts, pants... her essential clothing—and left for the trip.
questions.explanation: The first sentence lists three items separated by commas, uses an ellipsis after "pants" to show the omitted final item, and encloses the appositive "her essential clothing" with a pair of dashes.
questions.skill: Identify correct punctuation for pauses and omissions
questions.topic: Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly leaves a restrictive clause unpunctuated by commas and uses a dash to add emphasis to the final phrase?
choices: The students, who studied for the exam, passed easily—some in record time.
The students who studied for the exam, passed easily—some in record time.
The students who studied for the exam passed easily - some in record time.
The students who studied for the exam passed easily—some in record time.
questions.explanation: The restrictive clause who studied for the exam correctly takes no commas, and the em dash adds emphasis to some in record time.
questions.skill: Distinguishing restrictive clauses from nonrestrictive clauses
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to mark words left unstated at the end of a speaker's thought?
choices: Either you apologize, or— Eli said, though he did not finish the warning.
Either you apologize, or, Eli said, though he did not finish the warning.
Either you apologize, or: Eli said, though he did not finish the warning.
Either you apologize, or... Eli said, though he did not finish the warning.
questions.explanation: The ellipsis marks the unstated alternative that Eli leaves unexpressed in his warning.
questions.skill: Using ellipses in unfinished speech
questions.topic: Activity 7 of 9 (quiz/game): Write Your Own (Rubric Check) - Ellipses, Dashes, and Commas for Pauses and Omissions

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a pair of commas to set off a nonrestrictive clause, an ellipsis to omit words at the end of a quotation, and a dash to add emphasis before a final independent clause?
choices: The professor, who had taught for decades, said, 'Remember the deadline...' the class fell silent, and everyone took notes.
